claims.text: Machine-learning-guided sputter deposition can produce nanostructured coatings on stainless steel.
Such coatings significantly improve stainless-steel corrosion resistance in extreme environments.
Conventional stainless steel is vulnerable to severe corrosion because of its surface composition and microstructure.
Machine-learning models can optimize the processing parameters and composition of a sputter-deposited coating.
High-temperature or high-salt media can constitute extreme corrosive environments for stainless steel.
The proposed process forms a nanostructured surface layer.
The proposed process forms a dense and chemically passivating surface layer.
The surface layer has an optimized phase composition.
Machine-learning optimization ensures that the coating is uniformly dense and chemically inert.
The dense, chemically inert coating acts as a barrier to corrosive agents.
Corrosive species and impurities can cause elemental dissolution or leaching from stainless steel in molten salt.
The coating reduces elemental dissolution and the overall corrosion rate.
Coated samples will have a lower corrosion rate than unmodified stainless-steel samples.
The coating may reduce corrosion metrics by approximately 20–30%.
Unmodified stainless steel undergoes rapid degradation under extreme corrosive stress.
Substantial deviations from the machine-learning-optimized deposition parameters may diminish coating effectiveness.
Environmental aggressiveness beyond the designed operating window may diminish coating effectiveness.
The magnitude of corrosion improvement depends on deposition parameters, coating microstructure, and environmental variables.
Electrochemical testing, mass loss, and post-exposure surface characterization can compare corrosion performance and coating integrity between coated and uncoated samples.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement greater than 20% relative to an unmodified control would falsify the hypothesis.
